t: They have been neglecting maintenance of the archives for years. [Active → Passive]
o: Maintenance of the archives had been neglected by them for years.
Maintenance of the archives is being neglected by them for years.
Maintenance of the archives was being neglected by them for years.
Maintenance of the archives has been being neglected by them for years.
e: This tests Present Perfect Continuous Active ('has/have been + V-ing') converted to Passive, which becomes 'has/have been being + V3' -- another rare, grammatically valid but clunky double-auxiliary form (compare with the 'will be being' pattern above). Exams occasionally test whether you can recognise this construction even though native speakers avoid saying it aloud.

t: The university may confer honorary degrees upon exceptional scholars. [Active → Passive]
o: Honorary degrees might have been conferred upon exceptional scholars by the university.
Honorary degrees may be conferred upon exceptional scholars by the university.
Honorary degrees may have conferred upon exceptional scholars by the university.
Honorary degrees must be being conferred upon exceptional scholars by the university.
e: Rule: 'may + V1' becomes 'may be + V3' in Passive. 'may confer' turns into 'may be conferred'. Notice the preposition phrase 'upon exceptional scholars' stays attached right after the verb in exactly the same position.

t: Someone must have tampered with the encryption keys. [Active → Passive]
o: The encryption keys must have been tampered with.
must have tampered by someone.
must be tampered with by someone.
must had been tampered with.
e: Rule: Modal Perfect Active ('must have + V3') becomes 'must have been + V3' in Passive. 'must have tampered' turns into 'must have been tampered'. Since the doer is only the vague word 'someone', the agent is simply dropped. Also note the phrasal verb 'tamper with' keeps its preposition 'with' stuck to the verb -- it never moves anywhere else in the sentence.

t: Meenakshi could have sent a reply. [Active → Passive]
o: A reply could have be sent by Meenakshi.
A reply could have been sent by Meenakshi.
A reply could have sent by Meenakshi.
A reply could have been send by Meenakshi.
e: Same Modal Perfect rule as above: 'could have + V3' becomes 'could have been + V3'. 'could have sent' turns into 'could have been sent'. Look closely at the wrong options: one drops 'been' ('could have be sent'), one skips 'been' entirely ('could have sent' -- still sounds active), and one wrongly uses 'send' instead of the past participle 'sent'. Only the correct option has the full, correct chain: modal + have + been + V3.

t: Did you hear that noise? [Active → Passive]
o: Was that noise heard by you?
Is that noise heard by you?
Wasn't that noise heard by you?
Has that noise been heard by you?
e: Rule: 'Did + subject + V1...?' becomes 'Was/Were + object + V3 + by + subject?' in Passive. 'Did you hear' (base verb 'hear') turns into 'Was...heard' (past participle 'heard'). The question-word 'Did' disappears completely and is replaced by 'was', which now carries the past tense.

t: Why didn't she bring her son to my house? [Active → Passive]
o: Why wasn't her son brought by her to my house?
Why isn't her son brought to my house?
Why wasn't her son brought to my house?
Why isn't her son brought by you to my house?
e: Rule: 'didn't + V1' becomes 'wasn't + V3' in negative Simple Past Passive. 'didn't bring' turns into 'wasn't brought'. The question word 'Why' stays first, and 'by her' is kept here (rather than dropped) because the sentence is specifically about her not doing the action, so removing the agent would lose that focus.

t: I bade him write the composition twice. [Active → Passive]
o: He was bid to write the composition twice.
He was baden to write the composition twice.
He was bade to write the composition twice.
He was bidden to write the composition twice.
e: 'Bade' is the old-fashioned past tense of 'bid' (meaning 'ordered' or 'instructed'). In its passive form it stays as 'was/were bade + to-infinitive' -- notice it keeps the unusual spelling 'bade' rather than switching to a regular-looking form like 'bidden'. This is an archaic but exam-favourite irregular verb worth memorising as a special case.

t: Somebody sent him a cheque for a hundred euros as his remuneration. [Active → Passive]
o: He was sent a cheque for a hundred euros as his remuneration by someone.
He was been sent a cheque for a hundred euros as his remuneration by someone.
He sent a cheque for a hundred euros as his remuneration.
He is sent a cheque for a hundred euros as his remuneration by someone.
e: Rule: With ditransitive verbs (verbs that take two objects, like send/give/offer/teach), you can passivise by turning the indirect object -- the receiver, 'him' -- into the subject: 'He was sent...'. The direct object (the thing given, 'a cheque') simply stays in place after the verb.

t: People say Shyam is wise and honest. [Active → Passive]
o: It is believed that Shyam is wise and honest.
Let's say that Shyam is wise and honest.
Shyam is wise and honest is said by people.
It is said that Shyam is wise and honest.
e: Rule: For reporting verbs like 'say/think/believe' followed by a 'that-clause', the standard passive pattern uses the dummy subject 'It': 'People say that...' turns into 'It is said that...'. The clause that follows ('Shyam is wise and honest') stays completely unchanged, since it is not the part being passivised.

t: It was decided by Salim Ali to devote his life to the preservation of Indian birds. [Passive → Active]
o: Salim Ali decided to devote his life to the preservation of Indian birds.
Salim devoted his life to the preservation of Indian birds.
Salim Ali has decided to devote his life to the preservation of Indian birds.
Salim Ali had decided to devote his life to the preservation of Indian birds.
e: Rule: The impersonal passive pattern 'It was decided by X to + V1' reverses simply to 'X decided to + V1' in Active -- both the dummy 'It' and 'by' disappear, and 'X' becomes an ordinary subject.

t: They should be auditing the subsidiary accounts this quarter. [Active → Passive]
o: The subsidiary accounts should have been audited this quarter.
The subsidiary accounts are being audited this quarter.
The subsidiary accounts should be being audited by them this quarter.
The subsidiary accounts should be audited by them this quarter.
e: This tests Modal Continuous Active ('should be + V-ing') converted to Passive, which becomes 'should be being + V3' -- a rare but grammatically correct double-auxiliary passive, similar to the 'will be being' and 'has been being' patterns seen in Set 1. 'should be auditing' turns into 'should be being audited'.

t: Bhavna saw him carrying your suitcase. [Active → Passive]
o: Your suitcase carried by him was seen by Bhavna.
He was seen by Bhavna carrying your suitcase.
He had been seen by Bhavna carrying your suitcase.
Your suitcase was seen by Bhavna carrying him.
e: Rule: With perception verbs (see/hear/watch + object + V-ing), the object of 'saw' ('him') becomes the subject of the passive sentence, and the '-ing' form ('carrying') stays exactly as it is right after 'seen'. 'saw him carrying' turns into 'was seen...carrying'.

t: Trigonometry has been taught by him for donkey's years. [Passive → Active]
o: He had been teaching trigonometry for donkey's years.
Trigonometry has been teaching by him for donkey's years.
He is teaching trigonometry for donkey's years.
He has been teaching trigonometry for donkey's years.
e: Rule: Present Perfect Passive ('has/have been + V3') reverses to Present Perfect Continuous Active ('has/have been + V-ing') when the sentence emphasises a long, ongoing duration -- signalled here by 'for donkey's years', an idiom meaning 'for a very long time'. 'has been taught' turns into 'has been teaching'.

t: The research team is conducting experiments on a new drug that could revolutionise the treatment of the disease. [Active → Passive]
o: Experiments are being conducted on a new drug that could revolutionise the treatment of the disease through the research team.
Experiments were being conducted on a new drug that could revolutionise the treatment of the disease by the research team.
Experiments are being conducted on a new drug that could revolutionise the treatment of the disease from the research team.
Experiments are being conducted on a new drug that could revolutionise the treatment of the disease by the research team.
e: This sentence has a relative clause, 'that could revolutionise...', which has its own subject 'that' referring back to 'drug' -- this clause is never touched during the conversion. Only the main clause, 'The research team is conducting experiments', is passivised: 'is conducting' turns into 'are being conducted', since the new subject 'experiments' is plural.

t: The company will launch the new product next month, and they are already promoting it through various marketing channels. [Active → Passive]
o: The new product will be launched by the company next month, and it is already being promoted through various marketing channels.
The new product were been launched by the company next month, and it was promoting it through various marketing channels.
The new product was launched by the company next month, and it is already promoted through various marketing channels.
The new product will have been launched by the company next month, and it was already being promoted through various marketing channels.
e: This is a compound sentence with two clauses joined by 'and' -- each clause keeps its own original tense when passivised. Clause 1 (Simple Future): 'will launch' turns into 'will be launched'. Clause 2 (Present Continuous): 'are promoting' turns into 'is being promoted', matching 'it' (the product, singular).

t: Lovely tunes are composed by Domnica. [Passive → Active]
o: Domnica composed lovely tunes.
Domnica composes tunes lovely.
Domnica will compose lovely tunes.
Domnica composes lovely tunes.
e: Rule: Simple Present Passive ('is/are + V3') reverses to plain V1 (with '-s' for a singular subject) in Active. 'are composed' turns into 'composes' -- the '-s' is added because the new subject 'Domnica' is third-person singular. The agent 'by Domnica' simply becomes the subject.

t: Scientists were conducting experiments on the newly discovered species. [Active → Passive]
o: Experiments had been conducted on the newly discovered species by scientists.
Experiments has been conducting on the newly discovered species by scientists.
Experiments has been experimented on the newly discovered species by scientists.
Experiments were being conducted on the newly discovered species by scientists.
e: Rule: Past Continuous Active ('was/were + V-ing') becomes 'was/were being + V3' in Passive. 'were conducting' turns into 'were being conducted' -- 'were' is used because the new subject 'experiments' is plural.

t: Gill scored 3 centuries in Tata IPL 2023. [Active → Passive]
o: 3 centuries has been scored by Gill in Tata IPL 2023.
3 centuries were scored by Gill in Tata IPL 2023.
3 centuries had been scored by Gill in Tata IPL 2023.
3 centuries were being scored by Gill in Tata IPL 2023.
e: Rule: Simple Past Active ('scored') becomes 'was/were + V3' in Passive. Since '3 centuries' is a plural quantity, the correct helping verb is 'were', not 'was' or 'has' -- always check whether the new subject is singular or plural before picking the auxiliary.

t: Neena will visit Greece in May. [Active → Passive]
o: Greece had been visited by Neena in May.
Greece has been visited by Neena in May.
Greece will be visited by Neena in May.
Greece will visit Neena in May.
e: Rule: Simple Future Active ('will + V1') becomes 'will be + V3' in Passive. 'will visit' turns into 'will be visited'. The time expression 'in May' stays at the end in both the active and passive versions.

t: The flood victims of Assam have to make highway their home every year. [Active → Passive]
o: Highway has made their home every year by the flood victims of Assam.
Highway has been made their home every year by the flood victims of Assam.
Highway is being made their home every year by the flood victims of Assam.
Highway has to be made their home every year by the flood victims of Assam.
e: Rule: Same 'have to' pattern as the previous question -- 'have to + V1' becomes 'has to be + V3' in Passive. 'have to make' turns into 'has to be made', since 'highway' is treated as singular/uncountable. The phrase 'their home every year' keeps its same position right after the verb.

t: I have to stay in Netherlands for a year till I finish my course. [Paraphrase]
o: I may be allowed to stay in Netherlands for a year till I finish my course.
It is suggested that I stay in Netherlands for a year till I finish my course.
I am obliged to stay in Netherlands for a year till I finish my course.
Let me stay in Netherlands for a year till I finish my course.
e: This isn't a literal active-to-passive conversion -- it tests recognising that 'have to' expresses obligation, which can be paraphrased using 'am/is/are obliged to' (a synonym phrase) while keeping the same meaning. The rest of the sentence, 'for a year till I finish my course', stays unchanged.

t: They had been making the staff report discrepancies silently. [Active → Passive]
o: The staff had been made to report discrepancies silently.
The staff were being made to report discrepancies silently.
Discrepancies had been reported by the staff silently.
The staff have been made to report discrepancies silently.
e: This tests recognising a hidden causative meaning: 'making the staff report' implies forcing or causing the staff to act, so the best passive keeps that causative sense with 'had been made to report' rather than simplifying it to a plain passive. This preserves the original meaning that someone was compelling the staff to act.

t: Ishika saw the tiger in the forest. [Active → Passive]
o: The tiger saw by Ishika in the forest.
The tiger was seen by the forest in Ishika.
The tiger was seen by Ishika in the forest.
The tiger sees Ishika in the forest.
e: Rule: Simple Past Active becomes 'was/were + V3' in Passive as usual: 'saw' turns into 'was seen'. The key trap here is word order -- the place phrase 'in the forest' must stay attached at the end, describing where the tiger was seen, and should never be scrambled elsewhere in the sentence.

t: Nargis quickly picks out the important files from her office shelf. [Active → Passive]
o: The important files are quickly being picked out by Nargis from her office shelf.
The important files will be quickly picked out by Nargis from her office shelf.
The important files are quickly picked out by Nargis from her office shelf.
The important files have quickly been picked out by Nargis from her office shelf.
e: Rule: Simple Present Active ('picks') becomes 'are picked' in Passive, since the new subject 'files' is plural. Two things must stay intact: the phrasal verb 'pick out' (both words move together and are never split apart), and the adverb 'quickly', which sits right before the verb -- 'are quickly picked out' -- in the passive version.

t: People don't use this road much. [Active → Passive]
o: This road isn't much used by people.
This road cannot be used much by people.
This road isn't used much by public.
This road isn't used much.
e: Rule: When the doer ('people' = everyone in general) is too obvious or unimportant to mention, it is completely dropped in Passive rather than written as 'by people'. 'don't use...much' turns into 'isn't used much', with the adverb 'much' staying close to the verb.

t: People consider that Radha is creative in her work. [Active → Passive]
o: Radha's creativity in her work is considered by others.
It is considered that Radha is creative in her work.
Creativity in work by Radha is considered by people.
People have considered Radha's creativity in her work.
e: Rule: Just like 'People say that...' turns into 'It is said that...', the reporting verb 'consider' followed by a 'that-clause' uses the dummy subject 'It' in Passive: 'People consider that...' turns into 'It is considered that...'. The clause that follows, 'Radha is creative in her work', stays exactly the same.

t: He likes people to flatter him. [Active → Passive]
o: He likes people to be flattered by him.
He likes to have been flattered by people.
He liked to be flattered by people.
He likes to be flattered by people.
e: Same 'like/want/wish + object + to + V1' pattern as the previous question: the object of 'likes' ('people...him') is restructured, with the doer becoming the agent 'by people' and the receiver 'him' disappearing since it's now the implied subject of 'to be flattered'. 'likes people to flatter him' turns into 'likes to be flattered by people'.

t: His mother accompanies him wherever he goes. [Active → Passive]
o: He has accompanied his mother wherever she has gone.
He was accompanied by his mother wherever he went.
He is accompanied by his mother wherever he goes.
He accompanies his mother wherever she goes.
e: Rule: Only the main clause subject and object swap here ('his mother' and 'him' turn into 'is accompanied by his mother'). The clause 'wherever he goes' has its own independent subject 'he' (referring to the son, not the mother), so it must stay exactly as 'he goes' -- it should never be changed to 'she goes'.

t: Editors deem such practices incompatible with editorial ethics. [Active → Passive]
o: Such practices are deemed incompatible with editorial ethics.
Editorial ethics deems such practices as incompatible.
Editors have deemed editorial ethics incompatible with such practices.
Editorial compatibility is deemed absent in such practices.
e: Rule: With verbs like 'deem/consider/regard' that take an object plus a complement ('object + incompatible with...'), the object becomes the subject in Passive, and the complement phrase stays attached right after the verb. 'deem such practices incompatible' turns into 'such practices are deemed incompatible'.

t: Change the following from active to passive: The professor could have been explaining differential topology for hours.
o: Differential topology could have be being explained for hours by the professor.
Differential topology could have explained for hours by the professor.
Differential topology could have been being explained for hours by the professor.
Differential topology could have had been been explained for hours by the professor.
e: could have been explaining → could have been being explained. Option A mein been ki jagah be likha hai jo galat hai. Option D mein do baar been been likha hai. Option C bilkul perfect hai.

t: Change the following from active to passive: They may have been undervaluing the intellectual property portfolio.
o: The intellectual property portfolio may have be being undervalued.
The intellectual property portfolio may have undervalued.
The intellectual property portfolio may have been being undervalued.
The intellectual property portfolio may have had been been undervalued.
e: Active mein may have been undervaluing hai. Passive banega: may have been + being undervalued.

t: Change the following from active to passive: The advisory panel might have been overlooking critical discrepancies in the data prior to the audit.
o: Critical discrepancies in the data might have been being overlooked by the advisory panel prior to the audit.
Critical discrepancies were being overlooked by the panel prior to the audit.
Critical discrepancies might have overlooked the panel during the audit.
Critical discrepancies had been overlooked by the panel during the audit.
e: Bada sentence dekh kar darna nahi hai, sirf verb pakdo. might have been overlooking might have been being overlooked. Baaki saara sentence → as it is jaha ka waha rahega.

t: Change the following sentence from active to passive: "The principal investigator might have been continuously analyzing the erratic fluctuations in the molecular structure caused by high-frequency radiation during the controlled simulations."
o: The fluctuations in molecular structure might have been continuously analyzed by the principal investigator during the simulations.
The erratic fluctuations caused by high-frequency radiation might have been continuously under analysis by the principal investigator during the controlled simulations.
During the controlled simulations, the erratic fluctuations in the molecular structure were continuously analyzed by the principal investigator.
Continuous analysis of the fluctuations in molecular structure by the principal investigator might have been performed during the controlled simulations.
e: Yeh thoda hatke question hai. Technical rule ke hisaab se answer hona chahiye tha might have been being continuously analyzed. Lekin SSC ne options mein being wala exact format diya hi nahi! Jab options standard grammar rule follow na karein, toh humein meaning ko preserve karne wala "best fit" option chunna hota hai. Yahan "continuously under analysis" use karke continuous action ka meaning barkarar rakha gaya hai aur modal (might have been) bhi sahi hai. Isliye (b) best option hai.

t: Change the following from active to passive: The team will be revising the algorithms during the workshop.
o: The algorithms were being revised during the workshop.
The algorithms will be been revised during the workshop.
The algorithms will be revised during the workshop.
The algorithms will be being revised during the workshop.
e: Active: will be revising. Passive: will be being revised. Option C mein being miss kar diya gaya hai jo continuous aspect khatam kar deta hai.

t: Change the following from active to passive: Industry leaders have been challenging the proposed legislation for its lack of clarity and enforcement mechanisms.
o: The proposed legislation has been being challenged for its lack of clarity and enforcement mechanisms by industry leaders.
The proposed legislation was challenged by industry leaders for clarity and mechanism.
The legislation has been challenged by leaders for its lack of clarity.
The legislation is being challenged by industry leaders for its lack of clarity.
e: have been challenging has been being challenged (Kyunki 'legislation' singular → subject hai).

t: Change the following from active to passive: The think tank will have been reviewing policy outcomes across sectors by the end of the fiscal cycle.
o: Policy outcomes across sectors will have been being reviewed by the think tank by the end of the fiscal cycle.
Policy outcomes across sectors were reviewed by the think tank by the end of the fiscal cycle.
Policy outcomes across sectors will have been reviewed by the think tank by the end of the fiscal cycle.
Policy outcomes across sectors will be reviewed by the think tank by the end of the fiscal cycle.
e: Future Perfect Continuous will have been reviewing hai. Passive banega will have been + being reviewed. Option C mein being nahi hai isliye wo Future Perfect ka passive ban gaya, jabki humein Future Perfect *Continuous* chahiye.

t: Change the following from active to passive: The agency had been monitoring dissent groups covertly for months.
o: Dissent groups had covertly monitored the agency.
Dissent groups had been monitored covertly by the agency for months.
Covert monitoring had occurred over months.
The dissent groups were under surveillance.
e: ⚠️ Pro-Tip / Exception: Yahan dhyan dijiye! Technical rule ke hisaab se answer had been being monitored hona chahiye tha. Lekin SSC ne options mein being lagaya hi nahi! Jab options mein strictly perfect continuous ka passive na ho, toh hum use normal Past Perfect Passive (had been monitored) mein reduce kar dete hain. Baaki teeno options ka toh meaning hi galat nikal raha hai, isliye yahan best choice (b) hi bachti hai.

t: Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure: The documents have been being reviewed by the compliance team for several weeks.
o: The compliance team has reviewed the documents for weeks.
The compliance team has been reviewing the documents for several weeks.
The documents were being reviewed for several weeks.
The compliance team had reviewed the documents weekly.
e: Passive: have been being reviewed. Ise wapas active banane ke liye agent the compliance team (singular) aage laao. Phir have been being reviewed → has been reviewing ho jayega.

t: Convert from passive to active voice: The funds were believed to have been misallocated by certain board members over several quarters.
o: Certain board members believed to misallocate the funds.
Certain board members are believed to have misallocated the funds over several quarters.
It is believed that board members misallocate the funds.
Board members believed that funds were misallocated.
e: "Were believed" की जगह tense के flow को ठीक करने के लिए "are believed" लिया गया है। "to ave been misallocated by..." का Active "to have misallocated" h होगा और "Certain board members" आगे आ जाएं गे।

t: Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure: The evidence was presumed to have been fabricated before being presented in court.
o: It is presumed that someone had fabricated the evidence before presenting it in court.
The court presumed the evidence to be fabricated.
The evidence had been fabricated, the court presumed.
Fabrication of evidence was presumed to occur.
e: "Was presumed" को Active "presumed" में बदला गया है और Subject "the court" लगा दिया गया है। "to have been fabricated" को "to be fabricated" कर दिया गया।

t: Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure: The culprit is believed to have been hiding in the abandoned warehouse for weeks.
o: People believe the warehouse hid the culprit.
It is believed that someone hid the culprit in the warehouse.
The culprit is believed to have hidden himself in the warehouse.
It is believed that the culprit has been hiding in the warehouse for weeks.
e: "is believed to have been hiding" को आसान Active structure में "It is believed that..." + "the culprit has been hiding" (Present Perfect Continuous) कर दिया गया है।

t: Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure: The agreement was found to have been violated despite multiple warnings.
o: It was found that someone violated the agreement.
Authorities found that the agreement was being violated.
Authorities found the agreement had been violated.
It had been found that the agreement was violated.
e: "was found" → "Authorities found"। "to have been violated" (Past Perfect का सेन्स) → "had been violated"।

t: Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure: No efforts were seen to have been made by the officials to resolve the crisis.
o: It was seen that officials resolved the crisis.
Officials were seen resolving the crisis effortfully.
The officials seemed to have resolved the crisis.
It was seen that the officials had made no efforts to resolve the crisis.
e: "were seen" → "It was seen that"। "to have been made by the officials" → "the officials had made no efforts"।

t: Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure: The investigation was believed to have been compromised by internal leaks.
o: The investigation compromised internal leaks, as believed.
It was believed that internal leaks had compromised the investigation.
Someone believed the investigation was compromising leaks.
Internal leaks are believed to compromise the investigation.
e: "was believed to have been compromised" → "It was believed that" + "internal leaks had compromised"।

t: Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure: The machinery was known to have been operated manually during the testing phase.
o: Manual operators were known to test the machinery.
Someone was known to operate the machinery manually during testing.
It was known that the machinery had been manually tested.
It is known that someone manually operated the machinery during testing.
e: "was known" सेम रहेगा। "to have been operated" को "to operate" करें गे और Dummy subject "Someone" का यूज़ करें गे।

t: Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure: The candidates were found to have been submitting forged documents during verification.
o: The verification process found the candidates had submitted forged documents.
It was found that forged documents had been submitted by candidates.
The candidates were found submitting forgeries, as verified.
Officials found that the candidates had been submitting forged documents.
e: "were found" → "Officials found that"। "to have been submitting" (Perfect Continuous) "had been submitting"। →

t: Choose the correct passive voice transformation of the sentence: He claimed to have seen a rare species of bird during his expedition to the Amazon rainforest.
o: It was claimed by him that he had seen a rare species of bird during his expedition to the Amazon rainforest.
A rare species of bird was claimed to have been seen by him during his expedition to the Amazon rainforest.
A rare species of bird was seen by him during his expedition, it was claimed.
He claimed that a rare species of bird was seen by him during his expedition.
e: "He claimed" → "was claimed"। "to have seen" (Perfect Infinitive) → "to have been seen" (Passive Perfect Infinitive)।

t: Choose the correct passive voice transformation of the sentence: The CEO is expected to have brought about significant changes in the department by the end of the year.
o: Significant changes are expected to have been brought about in the department by the new CEO by the end of the year.
It is expected that significant changes will have been brought about by the new CEO by the end of the year.
Significant changes will have been brought about in the department by the new CEO by the end of the year.
The new CEO is expected that significant changes will be brought about by them.
e: Object "Significant changes" आगे आएगा। "to have brought about" → "to have been brought about"। "is expected" वैसे का वैसा "are expected" (plural के कारण) हो जायेगा।

t: Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure: The law is supposed to be enforced strictly in sensitive areas.
o: The law enforces itself strictly in sensitive areas.
It is supposed that someone strictly enforced the law.
Authorities are supposed to enforce the law strictly in sensitive areas.
Strict enforcement of law is supposed in sensitive regions.
e: "is supposed to be enforced" → "Authorities are supposed to enforce"। Law enforce करने का काम authorities का होता है, इसलिए उन्हें implied subject मान लिया।

t: Change the following from active to passive: Have the archivists digitized the medieval manuscripts yet?
o: Were the medieval manuscripts digitized by the archivists yet?
Have the medieval manuscripts been digitized by the archivists yet?
Are the medieval manuscripts being digitized by the archivists yet?
Had the medieval manuscripts been digitized by the archivists yet?
e: "Have + Subject + V3" (Present Perfect) का Passive "Have/Has + Object + been + V3" होगा।

t: Change the following from active to passive: The government is said to have downplayed the findings deliberately.
o: The findings are said to be downplayed by the government.
It is said that the findings were downplayed deliberately.
The findings are said to have been downplayed deliberately by the government.
Deliberate findings were said to be downplayed by the government.
e: "to have downplayed" → "to have been downplayed" (Perfect Infinitive Passive)। Subject "The findings" आगे आ जायेगा।

t: Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure: It is presumed that the documents had been tampered with by internal staff before the audit.
o: Internal staff had tampered with the documents before the audit.
The audit presumed tampering by staff.

Applying the same pattern: Active: "The sewage water smells foul." → Passive: "The sewage water is foul when it is smelt." However, the grammatical passive construction DOES exist for sensory verbs as demonstrated. Testbook's solution also supports Option C as the correct passive construction.

The Passive voice in this question is in Present Continuous tense. Thus, the Active voice will also be in Present Continuous.

It can be transformed into the structure: Subject + needs + to be + V³. The gerund form after “need” implies necessity in a passive sense. However, “needs being + V³” is grammatically incorrect in standard English. 📌 Application to the Given Question The aging infrastructure of the public sector bank needs renovating immediately. Here, “needs renovating” already has a passive sense (i.e., needs to be renovated). The correct equivalent passive structure is: “needs to be renovated.” Option (A) is incorrect because “to renovate” makes the subject perform the action. Option (C) is grammatically incorrect (“needs being renovated”). Therefore, Option (B) is the accurate passive form. 💡 Things to Remember / Exam Tips “Need + V-ing” often carries passive meaning. The correct expanded form is “need(s) to be + V³.” Avoid structures like “needs being + V³.” Ensure the subject is not shown performing the action if the meaning is passive.

t: Select the passive form of the following sentence: "Market analysts suggest that the fiscal stimulus package has failed to revive the MSME sector."

e: The Correct Ans is Option (D) 📌 Rule / Concept: Passive of Reporting Verbs (Present + Perfect Clause) With reporting verbs like suggest, believe, report, etc., in the simple present tense, the passive can be formed as: (1) It + is + V³ + that + clause or (2) Subject + is + V³ + to + have + V³ (if referring to prior action). However, when the subordinate clause already contains a perfect construction (has failed), it should generally remain unchanged in the “It is suggested that…” structure. Option (C) is grammatically incorrect because “failed” cannot be used in passive form. Hence, Option (D) is the most accurate passive reconstruction. 💡 Things to Remember / Exam Tips Use “It is + V³ + that…” for reporting verbs in present tense. Do not attempt to passivize intransitive verbs like “fail.” Maintain the original tense and aspect of the subordinate clause. Prefer grammatically natural constructions over structurally forced ones.

The passive structure becomes: Object + was/were + V³ (+ by + Subject). When the verb is followed by a preposition (e.g., laugh at, look into, depend on), the preposition must be retained in the passive form. The tense must remain unchanged. Usually, intransitive verbs (laugh) have no passive. However, if they are followed by a fixed preposition (laugh at), they become "transitive-equivalents." The Reason: In the passive, the preposition "at" must stay with the verb, even if "by" follows it immediately. Option (A) is the trap for those who think "at" is redundant. 📌 Application to the Given Question- The recovery agents laughed at the defaulter’s explanation. Here, “laughed at” is a prepositional verb in the simple past tense. “The defaulter’s explanation” is the object and becomes the subject in passive voice. Since it is singular, the correct auxiliary is “was.” The correct passive structure is: was + laughed at. Option (A) is incorrect because it omits the preposition “at.” Option (B) incorrectly changes the tense to past continuous. Option (D) shifts the tense to past perfect and omits the agent. 💡 Things to Remember / Exam Tips Do not drop prepositions in prepositional verbs while converting to passive. Maintain the original tense. Use was/were + V³ for simple past passive. Check for subject–verb agreement carefully.

Option (B) omits “to be,” making it less standard in formal grammar. Option (C) forms an awkward and incorrect structure (“being checked”). Option (D) changes the meaning by removing the continuous sense. 💡 Things to Remember / Exam Tips For “found + object + V-ing,” use “was/were found to be + V-ing” in passive. Maintain the tense. Preserve the continuous sense when present in the original sentence. Avoid dropping necessary infinitive markers in formal constructions.
